passages: Meta ( META ) is riding high on its Muse AI agent.
The app has hit the top spot on both Apple's App Store and Google's Play Store and, according to market intelligence firm Sensor Tower, reached 560,000 daily active users after just 11 days.
Yahoo Finance is not a broker-dealer or investment adviser and does not offer securities or cryptocurrencies for sale or facilitate trading.
When you first fire up Muse, you'll get the option to name the AI agent a custom name.
Muse suggested a few options, but I chose to stick to plain old Muse.
I even used Muse to help grab a new defense for my fantasy football team.
I connected the agent to my Yahoo Fantasy Football account, and it searched for the defenses with the highest projected scores for the coming week.
Since I could only claim them on waivers, Muse put in a waiver request for the Kansas City Chiefs and dropped Green Bay.
The next day, when the claims were processed, Muse slotted Kansas City into my lineup as my active defense.

A small avatar that looks like a mix between an Ewok from "Star Wars" and Finn from "Adventure Time" started tapping away on a tiny keyboard at the top of the screen, indicating that Muse was processing my request.
Muse navigated to Nintendo's site and started the purchasing process, giving me a heads up as it moved through various steps.

Once it got to the point where it needed to log into my Nintendo account, Muse asked for my information, noting that it would stay in secure storage and that the agent couldn't see or read what I typed.
OpenAI ( OPAI.PVT ), Anthropic ( ANTH.PVT ), Google ( GOOG , GOOGL ), and Amazon ( AMZN ) each offer their own agents, as do open-source firms.
What sets Muse apart, however, is its focus on the consumer market.
Speaking of which… I'm moving and still haven't nailed down a mover.
To celebrate my future fantasy win, I asked Muse to search for nearby restaurants that serve gluten-free beer.
While the agent provided two correct options, it also pulled up one spot that has been closed for years.
When I pointed that out, it apologized and said it initially relied on stale data.
If Meta can convince users to trust Muse, though, it could prove to be a major win for the company's AI ambitions moving forward.
The app's early success sent Meta stock soaring 11% on Monday , as the market digested the positive news.
More recently, Meta settled a massive social media addiction case with a group of state attorneys general, agreeing to pay upwards of $17 billion and change several business practices.
Muse found four different companies in my area and sent out my request for quotes.
About two minutes later, my phone was blowing up with calls from two of the movers.
One company offered a quote straight up, which Muse provided to me.
Strangely, Muse provided a number but then said to use a different number instead.
Muse then told me not to trust unverified numbers from it.
The idea is for Muse to get things done on your behalf.
That includes things like firing off emails, helping organize your schedule, and shopping for you.

Coinbase pays us for certain activity generated through this link. Prices displayed are informational. Meta ( META ) is riding high on its Muse AI agent. The app has hit the top spot on both Apple's App Store and Google's Play Store and, according to market intelligence firm Sensor Tower, reached 560,000 daily active users after just 11 days. The app's early success sent Meta stock soaring 11% on Monday , as the market digested the positive news. AI agents are the next step in the evolution of AI. Rather than being chatbots like ChatGPT or Claude, agents use AI models to get things done. They aren't new, either. OpenAI ( OPAI.PVT ), Anthropic ( ANTH.PVT ), Google ( GOOG , GOOGL ), and Amazon ( AMZN ) each offer their own agents, as do open-source firms. What sets Muse apart, however, is its focus on the consumer market. The idea is for Muse to get things done on your behalf. That includes things like firing off emails, helping organize your schedule, and shopping for you. I took the agent for a test run to see how it stacks up to the hype and came away impressed with how well it handled most of what I threw at it, even if it ran into a few hiccups along the way. When you first fire up Muse, you'll get the option to name the AI agent a custom name. Muse suggested a few options, but I chose to stick to plain old Muse. And then I got to work. I started out by asking the agent to provide me with hourly updates on the latest tech headlines from a variety of news sites, something that would instantly make my work life a bit easier. A small avatar that looks like a mix between an Ewok from "Star Wars" and Finn from "Adventure Time" started tapping away on a tiny keyboard at the top of the screen, indicating that Muse was processing my request. The agent then came back with a confirmation that it would provide the headlines and links to the appropriate sites, even noting that some required subscriptions to access the full articles. Not too shabby. I'm in the market for a new video game for my Nintendo Switch 2, so I figured, why not let Muse take the wheel and buy it for me? I asked the agent to get to it. Muse navigated to Nintendo's site and started the purchasing process, giving me a heads up as it moved through various steps. Once it got to the point where it needed to log into my Nintendo account, Muse asked for my information, noting that it would stay in secure storage and that the agent couldn't see or read what I typed. Muse moved forward with the purchase, breaking down the total cost, saying it would charge it to my credit card on file with Nintendo, and prompting me to hit the buy button. But it was also much slower than if I simply went to the Nintendo site myself and ordered the game. I could, however, see how this would be helpful for someone who was buying a number of disparate items for, say, a party or a big move. Speaking of which… I'm moving and still haven't nailed down a mover. So I asked Muse to help compare local moving companies and provide some quotes. The agent asked for my current address, where I'm moving to, the number of bedrooms in my current place, if there are any stairs or elevators, and for the email and phone number where prospective movers could reach me. Muse found four different companies in my area and sent out my request for quotes. About two minutes later, my phone was blowing up with calls from two of the movers. One company offered a quote straight up, which Muse provided to me. The other movers sent over emails. That's the exact kind of use case that would get me to use an AI agent in my personal life. It took the annoying task of searching for movers and turned it into a quick back and forth before I was flooded with quotes. I then decided I'd book a date night for my wife and me, giving Muse some basic ideas for what I was looking for. It followed up with four suggestions, one of which I ended up booking via the agent through OpenTable. I even used Muse to help grab a new defense for my fantasy football team. I connected the agent to my Yahoo Fantasy Football account, and it searched for the defenses with the highest projected scores for the coming week. Since I could only claim them on waivers, Muse put in a waiver request for the Kansas City Chiefs and dropped Green Bay. The next day, when the claims were processed, Muse slotted Kansas City into my lineup as my active defense. To celebrate my future fantasy win, I asked Muse to search for nearby restaurants that serve gluten-free beer. While the agent provided two correct options, it also pulled up one spot that has been closed for years. When I pointed that out, it apologized and said it initially relied on stale data. I then asked about a casual spot that I know serves gluten-free beer. Muse said it didn't see any mention of such a beer on the restaurant's site, and suggested I call to see if it's something they have, but don't list. Strangely, Muse provided a number but then said to use a different number instead. When I asked why the change, it said it simply made up the first phone number out of thin air and didn't confirm it. Muse then told me not to trust unverified numbers from it. Hallucinations, or instances in which AI models confidently provide incorrect responses as if they are facts, are a known issue throughout the industry. And while companies have implemented improvements such as retrieval-augmented generation to reduce hallucinations, they still make it difficult to trust AI outputs outright. Despite that, Muse generally proved to be a solid helper for a host of multi-step tasks. But the AI agent will have to overcome hesitancy among some users who question whether they should share more data with Meta than they already do on Facebook and Instagram. The company has faced criticism over the years for how it handles user information, and in 2019, it paid $5 billion to the FTC to settle claims related to privacy issues stemming from the Cambridge Analytica scandal. More recently, Meta settled a massive social media addiction case with a group of state attorneys general, agreeing to pay upwards of $17 billion and change several business practices. If Meta can convince users to trust Muse, though, it could prove to be a major win for the company's AI ambitions moving forward. Email Daniel Howley at dhowley@yahoofinance.com. Meta ( META ) is riding high on its Muse AI agent. The app has hit the top spot on both Apple's App Store and Google's Play Store and, according to market intelligence firm Sensor Tower, reached 560,000 daily active users after just 11 days.
The app's early success sent Meta stock soaring 11% on Monday , as the market digested the positive news.
AI agents are the next step in the evolution of AI. Rather than being chatbots like ChatGPT or Claude, agents use AI models to get things done.

They aren't new, either. OpenAI ( OPAI.PVT ), Anthropic ( ANTH.PVT ), Google ( GOOG , GOOGL ), and Amazon ( AMZN ) each offer their own agents, as do open-source firms. What sets Muse apart, however, is its focus on the consumer market.
The idea is for Muse to get things done on your behalf. That includes things like firing off emails, helping organize your schedule, and shopping for you.
I took the agent for a test run to see how it stacks up to the hype and came away impressed with how well it handled most of what I threw at it, even if it ran into a few hiccups along the way.
When you first fire up Muse, you'll get the option to name the AI agent a custom name. Muse suggested a few options, but I chose to stick to plain old Muse.

And then I got to work. I started out by asking the agent to provide me with hourly updates on the latest tech headlines from a variety of news sites, something that would instantly make my work life a bit easier. A small avatar that looks like a mix between an Ewok from "Star Wars" and Finn from "Adventure Time" started tapping away on a tiny keyboard at the top of the screen, indicating that Muse was processing my request.

The agent then came back with a confirmation that it would provide the headlines and links to the appropriate sites, even noting that some required subscriptions to access the full articles. Not too shabby.

I'm in the market for a new video game for my Nintendo Switch 2, so I figured, why not let Muse take the wheel and buy it for me? I asked the agent to get to it. Muse navigated to Nintendo's site and started the purchasing process, giving me a heads up as it moved through various steps. Once it got to the point where it needed to log into my Nintendo account, Muse asked for my information, noting that it would stay in secure storage and that the agent couldn't see or read what I typed.
Muse moved forward with the purchase, breaking down the total cost, saying it would charge it to my credit card on file with Nintendo, and prompting me to hit the buy button.

But it was also much slower than if I simply went to the Nintendo site myself and ordered the game. I could, however, see how this would be helpful for someone who was buying a number of disparate items for, say, a party or a big move.

Speaking of which… I'm moving and still haven't nailed down a mover. So I asked Muse to help compare local moving companies and provide some quotes. The agent asked for my current address, where I'm moving to, the number of bedrooms in my current place, if there are any stairs or elevators, and for the email and phone number where prospective movers could reach me.

Muse found four different companies in my area and sent out my request for quotes. About two minutes later, my phone was blowing up with calls from two of the movers. One company offered a quote straight up, which Muse provided to me. The other movers sent over emails.

That's the exact kind of use case that would get me to use an AI agent in my personal life. It took the annoying task of searching for movers and turned it into a quick back and forth before I was flooded with quotes.

I then decided I'd book a date night for my wife and me, giving Muse some basic ideas for what I was looking for. It followed up with four suggestions, one of which I ended up booking via the agent through OpenTable.

I even used Muse to help grab a new defense for my fantasy football team. I connected the agent to my Yahoo Fantasy Football account, and it searched for the defenses with the highest projected scores for the coming week. Since I could only claim them on waivers, Muse put in a waiver request for the Kansas City Chiefs and dropped Green Bay. The next day, when the claims were processed, Muse slotted Kansas City into my lineup as my active defense.

To celebrate my future fantasy win, I asked Muse to search for nearby restaurants that serve gluten-free beer. While the agent provided two correct options, it also pulled up one spot that has been closed for years. When I pointed that out, it apologized and said it initially relied on stale data.

I then asked about a casual spot that I know serves gluten-free beer. Muse said it didn't see any mention of such a beer on the restaurant's site, and suggested I call to see if it's something they have, but don't list.

Strangely, Muse provided a number but then said to use a different number instead. When I asked why the change, it said it simply made up the first phone number out of thin air and didn't confirm it. Muse then told me not to trust unverified numbers from it.

Hallucinations, or instances in which AI models confidently provide incorrect responses as if they are facts, are a known issue throughout the industry. And while companies have implemented improvements such as retrieval-augmented generation to reduce hallucinations, they still make it difficult to trust AI outputs outright.
Despite that, Muse generally proved to be a solid helper for a host of multi-step tasks.
But the AI agent will have to overcome hesitancy among some users who question whether they should share more data with Meta than they already do on Facebook and Instagram.

The company has faced criticism over the years for how it handles user information, and in 2019, it paid $5 billion to the FTC to settle claims related to privacy issues stemming from the Cambridge Analytica scandal.
More recently, Meta settled a massive social media addiction case with a group of state attorneys general, agreeing to pay upwards of $17 billion and change several business practices.
If Meta can convince users to trust Muse, though, it could prove to be a major win for the company's AI ambitions moving forward.

sources.title: Meta wants you to trust its Muse AI with your calendar, reminders, and bank accounts - Android Authority
passages: Muse could also support several connectors, including popular ones such as Gmail , Google Calendar, health apps like Peloton and HealthEx, and more.
The agent could also be able to connect with users’ card providers and bank accounts, track expenses, and even suggest canceling unused subscriptions to save money.
However, it’s also possible that Muse will simply use bank and card statements received via users’ email accounts to track expenses.
Meta’s Muse AI agent certainly looks like it could be packed with enough smarts and features to get things done.
However, Meta’s reputation for protecting user privacy is not impressive, to say the least.
It will be interesting to see whether the company’s agentic AI is widely adopted once it is actually released to the public.

However, Meta will apparently ask users to join a waitlist or enter an invite code before giving them access to Muse.

sources.title: Meta just launched a new AI generator, Muse Image, and users are already pushing back over use of their photos - TechCrunch
passages: Meta on Tuesday unveiled Muse Image, its new AI image generator built by Meta Superintelligence Labs, the company’s dedicated AI unit.
The feature, which was internally code-named Mango, is now available for free through the Meta AI app, as well as on Instagram Stories and WhatsApp.
The company also said Muse Video — presumably an AI video generator — is “already in development.” TechCrunch has reached out to Meta for more information.
Meta says use of the new AI model is free for “everyday creation,” though users will need a subscription plan once they exceed a certain limit.
Those effects include customizable filters that can modify existing photos.
Meta’s privacy record is one reason for users’ unease over Muse.

The company paid a then-record $5 billion fine to the FTC in 2019, after regulators found that the political consulting firm Cambridge Analytica had improperly harvested data from tens of millions of Facebook users — without their knowledge — to build voter-targeting profiles ahead of the 2016 U.S. election.
Facebook had known about the data misuse for years before it became public.
If you’re short on inspiration and can’t come up with original prompts on your own, Meta says that Muse comes with “presets” — prefabricated image prompts — to “spark ideas.”
Basically, Muse’s photo-tagging feature, which is opt-out by default, fits a pattern users and regulators have flagged before: broad use of people’s data unless they actively turn it off.
However, a particularly eyebrow-raising feature allows users to manipulate another Instagram user’s images with AI, as long as that user’s profile is public.
Meta claims users “have control” over this feature, noting that there are settings you can use to disable this kind of co-option of your pictures if you want to.

Meta policy states that “people may be able to create content with your Instagram content using AI features at Meta” and that “you will not be notified about content created using AI features at Meta.”
One is creating custom ads (AI has notably crept into advertising over the past year).
Another is experimenting with interior decorating ideas — in a promotional video, a user leverages Muse to see what a secondhand couch might look like in their garage.
Said one X user after The Verge first pointed out how potentially invasive this is: “Pulling real users into generated photos without explicit consent is a privacy landmine waiting to detonate.”

coreStoryFacts.text: Meta ( META ) is riding high on its Muse AI agent.
The app has hit the top spot on both Apple's App Store and Google's Play Store and, according to market intelligence firm Sensor Tower, reached 560,000 daily active users after just 11 days.
Yahoo Finance is not a broker-dealer or investment adviser and does not offer securities or cryptocurrencies for sale or facilitate trading.
When you first fire up Muse, you'll get the option to name the AI agent a custom name.
Muse suggested a few options, but I chose to stick to plain old Muse.
I even used Muse to help grab a new defense for my fantasy football team.
I connected the agent to my Yahoo Fantasy Football account, and it searched for the defenses with the highest projected scores for the coming week.
Since I could only claim them on waivers, Muse put in a waiver request for the Kansas City Chiefs and dropped Green Bay.
The next day, when the claims were processed, Muse slotted Kansas City into my lineup as my active defense.

A small avatar that looks like a mix between an Ewok from "Star Wars" and Finn from "Adventure Time" started tapping away on a tiny keyboard at the top of the screen, indicating that Muse was processing my request.
Muse navigated to Nintendo's site and started the purchasing process, giving me a heads up as it moved through various steps.

Once it got to the point where it needed to log into my Nintendo account, Muse asked for my information, noting that it would stay in secure storage and that the agent couldn't see or read what I typed.
OpenAI ( OPAI.PVT ), Anthropic ( ANTH.PVT ), Google ( GOOG , GOOGL ), and Amazon ( AMZN ) each offer their own agents, as do open-source firms.
What sets Muse apart, however, is its focus on the consumer market.
Speaking of which… I'm moving and still haven't nailed down a mover.
To celebrate my future fantasy win, I asked Muse to search for nearby restaurants that serve gluten-free beer.
While the agent provided two correct options, it also pulled up one spot that has been closed for years.
When I pointed that out, it apologized and said it initially relied on stale data.
If Meta can convince users to trust Muse, though, it could prove to be a major win for the company's AI ambitions moving forward.
The app's early success sent Meta stock soaring 11% on Monday , as the market digested the positive news.
More recently, Meta settled a massive social media addiction case with a group of state attorneys general, agreeing to pay upwards of $17 billion and change several business practices.
Muse found four different companies in my area and sent out my request for quotes.
About two minutes later, my phone was blowing up with calls from two of the movers.
One company offered a quote straight up, which Muse provided to me.

That includes things like firing off emails, helping organize your schedule, and shopping for you. I took the agent for a test run to see how it stacks up to the hype and came away impressed with how well it handled most of what I threw at it, even if it ran into a few hiccups along the way. When you first fire up Muse, you'll get the option to name the AI agent a custom name. Muse suggested a few options, but I chose to stick to plain old Muse. And then I got to work. A small avatar that looks like a mix between an Ewok from "Star Wars" and Finn from "Adventure Time" started tapping away on a tiny keyboard at the top of the screen, indicating that Muse was processing my request. The agent then came back with a confirmation that it would provide the headlines and links to the appropriate sites, even noting that some required subscriptions to access the full articles. Once it got to the point where it needed to log into my Nintendo account, Muse asked for my information, noting that it would stay in secure storage and that the agent couldn't see or read what I typed. Muse moved forward with the purchase, breaking down the total cost, saying it would charge it to my credit card on file with Nintendo, and prompting me to hit the buy button. But it was also much slower than if I simply went to the Nintendo site myself and ordered the game. I could, however, see how this would be helpful for someone who was buying a number of disparate items for, say, a party or a big move. Speaking of which… I'm moving and still haven't nailed down a mover. So I asked Muse to help compare local moving companies and provide some quotes. The agent asked for my current address, where I'm moving to, the number of bedrooms in my current place, if there are any stairs or elevators, and for the email and phone number where prospective movers could reach me. Muse found four different companies in my area and sent out my request for quotes. About two minutes later, my phone was blowing up with calls from two of the movers. One company offered a quote straight up, which Muse provided to me. The other movers sent over emails. That's the exact kind of use case that would get me to use an AI agent in my personal life. It took the annoying task of searching for movers and turned it into a quick back and forth before I was flooded with quotes. I then decided I'd book a date night for my wife and me, giving Muse some basic ideas for what I was looking for. It followed up with four suggestions, one of which I ended up booking via the agent through OpenTable. I even used Muse to help grab a new defense for my fantasy football team. While the agent provided two correct options, it also pulled up one spot that has been closed for years. When I pointed that out, it apologized and said it initially relied on stale data. I then asked about a casual spot that I know serves gluten-free beer. Muse said it didn't see any mention of such a beer on the restaurant's site, and suggested I call to see if it's something they have, but don't list. Strangely, Muse provided a number but then said to use a different number instead. When I asked why the change, it said it simply made up the first phone number out of thin air and didn't confirm it. Muse then told me not to trust unverified numbers from it. Hallucinations, or instances in which AI models confidently provide incorrect responses as if they are facts, are a known issue throughout the industry. And while companies have implemented improvements such as retrieval-augmented generation to reduce hallucinations, they still make it difficult to trust AI outputs outright. Meta ( META ) is riding high on its Muse AI agent. The app has hit the top spot on both Apple's App Store and Google's Play Store and, according to market intelligence firm Sensor Tower, reached 560,000 daily active users after just 11 days.
The app's early success sent Meta stock soaring 11% on Monday , as the market digested the positive news.
AI agents are the next step in the evolution of AI. Rather than being chatbots like ChatGPT or Claude, agents use AI models to get things done.

They aren't new, either. OpenAI ( OPAI.PVT ), Anthropic ( ANTH.PVT ), Google ( GOOG , GOOGL ), and Amazon ( AMZN ) each offer their own agents, as do open-source firms. What sets Muse apart, however, is its focus on the consumer market.
The idea is for Muse to get things done on your behalf. That includes things like firing off emails, helping organize your schedule, and shopping for you.
I took the agent for a test run to see how it stacks up to the hype and came away impressed with how well it handled most of what I threw at it, even if it ran into a few hiccups along the way.
When you first fire up Muse, you'll get the option to name the AI agent a custom name. Muse suggested a few options, but I chose to stick to plain old Muse.

And then I got to work. I started out by asking the agent to provide me with hourly updates on the latest tech headlines from a variety of news sites, something that would instantly make my work life a bit easier. A small avatar that looks like a mix between an Ewok from "Star Wars" and Finn from "Adventure Time" started tapping away on a tiny keyboard at the top of the screen, indicating that Muse was processing my request.

The agent then came back with a confirmation that it would provide the headlines and links to the appropriate sites, even noting that some required subscriptions to access the full articles. Not too shabby.

I'm in the market for a new video game for my Nintendo Switch 2, so I figured, why not let Muse take the wheel and buy it for me? I asked the agent to get to it. Muse navigated to Nintendo's site and started the purchasing process, giving me a heads up as it moved through various steps. Once it got to the point where it needed to log into my Nintendo account, Muse asked for my information, noting that it would stay in secure storage and that the agent couldn't see or read what I typed.
Muse moved forward with the purchase, breaking down the total cost, saying it would charge it to my credit card on file with Nintendo, and prompting me to hit the buy button.

But it was also much slower than if I simply went to the Nintendo site myself and ordered the game. I could, however, see how this would be helpful for someone who was buying a number of disparate items for, say, a party or a big move.

Speaking of which… I'm moving and still haven't nailed down a mover. So I asked Muse to help compare local moving companies and provide some quotes. The agent asked for my current address, where I'm moving to, the number of bedrooms in my current place, if there are any stairs or elevators, and for the email and phone number where prospective movers could reach me.

Muse found four different companies in my area and sent out my request for quotes. About two minutes later, my phone was blowing up with calls from two of the movers. One company offered a quote straight up, which Muse provided to me. The other movers sent over emails.

That's the exact kind of use case that would get me to use an AI agent in my personal life. It took the annoying task of searching for movers and turned it into a quick back and forth before I was flooded with quotes.

I then decided I'd book a date night for my wife and me, giving Muse some basic ideas for what I was looking for. It followed up with four suggestions, one of which I ended up booking via the agent through OpenTable.

I even used Muse to help grab a new defense for my fantasy football team. I connected the agent to my Yahoo Fantasy Football account, and it searched for the defenses with the highest projected scores for the coming week. Since I could only claim them on waivers, Muse put in a waiver request for the Kansas City Chiefs and dropped Green Bay. The next day, when the claims were processed, Muse slotted Kansas City into my lineup as my active defense.

To celebrate my future fantasy win, I asked Muse to search for nearby restaurants that serve gluten-free beer. While the agent provided two correct options, it also pulled up one spot that has been closed for years. When I pointed that out, it apologized and said it initially relied on stale data.

I then asked about a casual spot that I know serves gluten-free beer. Muse said it didn't see any mention of such a beer on the restaurant's site, and suggested I call to see if it's something they have, but don't list.

Strangely, Muse provided a number but then said to use a different number instead. When I asked why the change, it said it simply made up the first phone number out of thin air and didn't confirm it. Muse then told me not to trust unverified numbers from it.

Hallucinations, or instances in which AI models confidently provide incorrect responses as if they are facts, are a known issue throughout the industry. And while companies have implemented improvements such as retrieval-augmented generation to reduce hallucinations, they still make it difficult to trust AI outputs outright.
Despite that, Muse generally proved to be a solid helper for a host of multi-step tasks.
But the AI agent will have to overcome hesitancy among some users who question whether they should share more data with Meta than they already do on Facebook and Instagram.

The company has faced criticism over the years for how it handles user information, and in 2019, it paid $5 billion to the FTC to settle claims related to privacy issues stemming from the Cambridge Analytica scandal.
More recently, Meta settled a massive social media addiction case with a group of state attorneys general, agreeing to pay upwards of $17 billion and change several business practices.
If Meta can convince users to trust Muse, though, it could prove to be a major win for the company's AI ambitions moving forward.

sources.title: Meta just launched a new AI generator, Muse Image, and users are already pushing back over use of their photos - TechCrunch
passages: Meta on Tuesday unveiled Muse Image, its new AI image generator built by Meta Superintelligence Labs, the company’s dedicated AI unit.
The feature, which was internally code-named Mango, is now available for free through the Meta AI app, as well as on Instagram Stories and WhatsApp.
The company also said Muse Video — presumably an AI video generator — is “already in development.” TechCrunch has reached out to Meta for more information.
Meta says use of the new AI model is free for “everyday creation,” though users will need a subscription plan once they exceed a certain limit.
Those effects include customizable filters that can modify existing photos.
Meta’s privacy record is one reason for users’ unease over Muse.

The company paid a then-record $5 billion fine to the FTC in 2019, after regulators found that the political consulting firm Cambridge Analytica had improperly harvested data from tens of millions of Facebook users — without their knowledge — to build voter-targeting profiles ahead of the 2016 U.S. election.
Facebook had known about the data misuse for years before it became public.
If you’re short on inspiration and can’t come up with original prompts on your own, Meta says that Muse comes with “presets” — prefabricated image prompts — to “spark ideas.”
Basically, Muse’s photo-tagging feature, which is opt-out by default, fits a pattern users and regulators have flagged before: broad use of people’s data unless they actively turn it off.
However, a particularly eyebrow-raising feature allows users to manipulate another Instagram user’s images with AI, as long as that user’s profile is public.
Meta claims users “have control” over this feature, noting that there are settings you can use to disable this kind of co-option of your pictures if you want to.

Meta policy states that “people may be able to create content with your Instagram content using AI features at Meta” and that “you will not be notified about content created using AI features at Meta.”
One is creating custom ads (AI has notably crept into advertising over the past year).
Another is experimenting with interior decorating ideas — in a promotional video, a user leverages Muse to see what a secondhand couch might look like in their garage.
Said one X user after The Verge first pointed out how potentially invasive this is: “Pulling real users into generated photos without explicit consent is a privacy landmine waiting to detonate.”

extraction.body: Meta on Tuesday unveiled Muse Image, its new AI image generator built by Meta Superintelligence Labs, the company’s dedicated AI unit. The feature, which was internally code-named Mango, is now available for free through the Meta AI app, as well as on Instagram Stories and WhatsApp. Unfortunately, the new model is already causing controversy. What exactly can you do with Muse? It sounds like the use cases are similar to most other AI image generators — you’ll be able to create plenty of goofy, cartoonish images, for instance. If you’re short on inspiration and can’t come up with original prompts on your own, Meta says that Muse comes with “presets” — prefabricated image prompts — to “spark ideas.” However, a particularly eyebrow-raising feature allows users to manipulate another Instagram user’s images with AI, as long as that user’s profile is public. Users merely tag the person, and it allows them to take their picture and use it to create a new AI image. Said one X user after The Verge first pointed out how potentially invasive this is: “Pulling real users into generated photos without explicit consent is a privacy landmine waiting to detonate.” Meta policy states that “people may be able to create content with your Instagram content using AI features at Meta” and that “you will not be notified about content created using AI features at Meta.” Meta claims users “have control” over this feature, noting that there are settings you can use to disable this kind of co-option of your pictures if you want to. Muse has other, less invasive applications. One is creating custom ads (AI has notably crept into advertising over the past year). Another is experimenting with interior decorating ideas — in a promotional video, a user leverages Muse to see what a secondhand couch might look like in their garage. This last function is designed to integrate with Facebook Marketplace, Meta’s popular Craigslist-like locus of used furniture and accessories. The model also features prompt-based image editing, which lets users create images to share across Meta’s apps and platforms. “Ask it to mock up an image of you in front of a historical landmark, cleanly erase a photobomber from the background of a shot, or write a custom prompt to build a functional QR code,” the company offers. At the same time, Meta is launching a host of new AI effects for Instagram Stories, powered by Muse — notably, the same platform at the center of the photo-tagging concerns above. Those effects include customizable filters that can modify existing photos. Meta says use of the new AI model is free for “everyday creation,” though users will need a subscription plan once they exceed a certain limit. The company also said Muse Video — presumably an AI video generator — is “already in development.” TechCrunch has reached out to Meta for more information. Meta has released a number of AI apps and services over the past year, including an AI assistant called Creator , and Pocket , an app that can be used to vibe-code video games. The company has been accused of having a nebulous AI strategy , although it’s still on track to spend a whole lot on AI infrastructure this year as it continues to build out its services. Meta’s privacy record is one reason for users’ unease over Muse. The company paid a then-record $5 billion fine to the FTC in 2019, after regulators found that the political consulting firm Cambridge Analytica had improperly harvested data from tens of millions of Facebook users — without their knowledge — to build voter-targeting profiles ahead of the 2016 U.S. election. Facebook had known about the data misuse for years before it became public. Separately, the company shut down Facebook’s facial-recognition system in 2021 — a tool that had automatically recognized people in photos and videos — amid lawsuits and regulatory pressure over its collection of biometric data. Basically, Muse’s photo-tagging feature, which is opt-out by default, fits a pattern users and regulators have flagged before: broad use of people’s data unless they actively turn it off. The company announced the feature on Thursday as part of a broader push to reduce friction in the ordering process.
DoorDash's move into conversational AI ordering puts it alongside competitors making similar investments.

All three companies are betting that conversational interfaces will become the default way consumers interact with delivery platforms, with the competitive stakes now extending beyond speed and price to which platform controls the initial purchase decision.
The launch follows a period of heavy investment at DoorDash.
In May, the company introduced AI tools for merchants.

It has also expanded into autonomous delivery technology including robots and completed two significant acquisitions: SevenRooms, a restaurant reservation platform, for $1.2 billion, and Deliveroo, a UK-based food delivery company, in a transaction valued at nearly $4 billion.

Chief Financial Officer Ravi Inukonda told investors during the company's most recent earnings call that DoorDash is making progress on a technology overhaul and expects most of the associated spending to occur this year, according to CNBC.

Andy Fang, Co-founder of DoorDash, described the intent behind the product: "We've spent over a decade building an app that puts everything in your city at your fingertips, but more options shouldn't mean more work.

DoorDash shares have fallen roughly 33 percent this year, compared with a gain of about 8 percent for the Nasdaq.
The decline was sharpest after the company disclosed late last year that it planned to spend "several hundred million dollars" on new products and technology in 2026.

passages: DoorDash has launched a new way to order food that skips the app entirely: texting an AI agent directly through Apple's Messages app.

DoorDash's AI agent searches local restaurants, scans menus, and builds a suggested cart based on the request, even sending photos of recommended dishes pulled directly from a restaurant's DoorDash shopfront.
The whole ordering process takes place without having to launch the DoorDash app at all.
The user just confirms their order through the chat window.
The more a person orders, the better the agent understands their habits and is even able to send a text message asking if they need their regular coffee order.
The AI agent will be able to deal with each individual’s request in one order, obviating the necessity of a particular person coordinating it manually.
Ordering as a group, usually a complicated logistics problem when you have to cater to various dietary needs and different amounts of food, becomes part of the same text-based interface.
The feature is currently limited to a waitlist for US users.
DoorDash hasn't specified a firm timeline for rollout, noting that access could arrive quickly or take longer dependin
Users simply text what they're craving, whether that's a specific dish, a mood-based recommendation, or a repeat of a regular order.

DoorDash, the San Francisco-based food and grocery delivery platform, has launched Ask DoorDash, an AI-powered chatbot that allows customers to describe what they want in plain language or upload photos to receive recommendations and place orders.

DoorDash's move into conversational AI ordering puts it alongside competitors making similar investments.

All three companies are betting that conversational interfaces will become the default way consumers interact with delivery platforms, with the competitive stakes now extending beyond speed and price to which platform controls the initial purchase decision.

In May, the company introduced AI tools for merchants.

sources.title: Airbnb adds direct messaging, new social features after app overhaul - cnbc.com
passages: Airbnb is adding new social features to its platform that allow guests attending experiences to communicate and keep in touch.

Business chief Dave Stephenson said the updated tech builds on the company's "vision for where to take Airbnb next." Users need to opt in to social features for every experience and can unsubscribe at any time, Airbnb said.
At the time of the May app overhaul, Stephenson told CNBC that Airbnb felt it had a "strong foundation" to expand its offerings.
The new updates add a direct messaging feature for attendees to connect with other guests and a pre-event dashboard that shows profiles of other participants attending the experience.
Earlier this year, Airbnb said it would invest $200 million to $250 million in a new business opportunities.
Airbnb also updated its artificial intelligence chatbot it started rolling out this year to answer personalized customer support questions.
The tool can now cancel reservations or adjust dates when prompted and is available in English, Spanish and French to users in North America.

extraction.body: Airbnb is evolving in two directions: On the ground, it wants to compete with hotels by providing myriad services; online, it is using AI and people in its Airbnb network to aid travel discovery. As part of its fall product update, the company is adding services to the app it had launched last year, such as meal delivery, laundry, baby-gear rental, ski and boat rental in limited locations, and expanded grocery delivery. The second big feature is AI search. The company has taken a cautious approach to rolling out AI features, with CEO Brian Chesky opting to stay away from a chatbot-like interface . Earlier this year, he teased the new search feature for property discovery . Now, users can switch on a toggle to search for properties via text or voice prompts. Once you start the search, the interface will show you dynamic filters based on your preferences. For instance, if you type “baby” in the AI search filter, Airbnb will automatically show you further filters like cribs, playgrounds, or children’s books and toys. The platform is also using AI to bring out relevant features of a property, and will let you compare properties in your wish list by way of AI-powered summaries and reviews. “We are finally making our first foray into AI search. And what you see is just the very beginning of something. And over the coming months, we’re going to really be iterating this very quickly. It’s not hard to create AI search; it’s hard to create AI search in e-commerce when you have $100 billion going through your platform,” Airbnb CEO Brian Chesky told TechCrunch. “Anyone can vibe-code a search function, but to do something that doesn’t kill conversion rate, that’s the hard part.” The company is also doubling down on social features that nudge people to take more trips and book additional experiences such as food tastings and craft workshops. Last year, the app started allowing users to connect with fellow travelers and friends on its platform. Now, travelers can look at a map based on their connections’ past or upcoming trips. When you tap on a trip, you can see where your connection stayed, and which experiences they sought out. For those conscious about their privacy, there’s an option to not share their trips with others as well. Airbnb is also building pages about neighborhoods based on guest reviews and other sources to help travelers discover places to eat and things to do. passages: Airbnb on September 30, 2026 announced its 2026 fall update , adding AI-powered search and trip-planning tools, social features for discovering destinations through personal connections, and new services including meal delivery, laundry, and baby gear rentals.

The company said the features start rolling out with the announcement, with the new AI capabilities launching in the United States first, additional service categories arriving through later this year, and a set of AI-powered host tools scheduled for later this fall.

Search results now include AI-powered listing descriptions highlighting key features of a home, and an AI-powered comparison tool displays homes from a user’s wishlist side by side, with AI summaries of their key features.
Connected trips appear on an interactive Travel Map showing where connections have traveled and where they are going next.

In its Help Center documentation , Airbnb states that AI-powered search considers factors including quality, popularity, price, and location, and that AI also supports personalization, customer support, and guest-host communications such as suggested quick replies for hosts.
Airbnb says that, starting in the US, it is bringing AI into every step of a trip, from planning through check-in.
A new search bar lets users search across homes, experiences, and services in their own words or by voice.

Within filters, users can now type keywords and instantly see matching options; the company gives the example of typing “baby” to surface related filters such as cribs, playgrounds, or children’s books and toys, without scrolling through filter lists.
Laundry pickup and delivery is available in select US cities through a partnership with Rinse, with Airbnb guests receiving free pickup, delivery, and next-day rush service.
Additional services through local partners include ski and snowboard gear rentals in the French Alps and boat rentals in South Florida.

The company said the features start rolling out with the announcement, with the new AI capabilities launching in the United States first, additional service categories arriving through later this year, and a set of AI-powered host tools scheduled for later this fall. The update follows Airbnb’s 2026 summer release earlier this year, which the company described as adding even more ways to travel on the platform. A new Connect feature lets users invite family, friends, and people they have traveled with to connect on Airbnb. Once connected, each side can see the other’s trips, and Airbnb says it will also suggest connections based on a user’s past trips. Connected trips appear on an interactive Travel Map showing where connections have traveled and where they are going next. Users can explore where a connection stayed and which experiences or services they booked, read their reviews, save favorites to a wishlist, or message them directly in the app, with the map filling in as more connections are added. Privacy controls let users decide which trips appear on their travel map and how much of each trip is shared, and a trip can be hidden or removed, or a connection blocked, at any time. Tapping the map opens neighborhood pages that provide an overview of an area, built from what guests and hosts tell Airbnb and from other sources. The pages cover what a neighborhood is like, things to do, where to eat, and how to get around, and they include top experiences and services from local hosts. Airbnb says that, starting in the US, it is bringing AI into every step of a trip, from planning through check-in. A new search bar lets users search across homes, experiences, and services in their own words or by voice. Within filters, users can now type keywords and instantly see matching options; the company gives the example of typing “baby” to surface related filters such as cribs, playgrounds, or children’s books and toys, without scrolling through filter lists. Search results now include AI-powered listing descriptions highlighting key features of a home, and an AI-powered comparison tool displays homes from a user’s wishlist side by side, with AI summaries of their key features. On the support side, Airbnb says AI-powered chat support is now available in more than 50 languages, and the company is expanding the capability to voice so guests can get quick answers over the phone. In its Help Center documentation , Airbnb states that AI-powered search considers factors including quality, popularity, price, and location, and that AI also supports personalization, customer support, and guest-host communications such as suggested quick replies for hosts. The company says personal information may be used to develop and improve the AI models behind these features, citing safeguards such as de-identification, data encryption, and pseudonymization, and that users can turn off that data sharing through a “Help improve AI-powered features” control in their account privacy settings. Airbnb is expanding Airbnb Services into new categories starting with the announcement and continuing through later this year. Meal delivery from local restaurants to a guest’s listing is available in select cities across Europe, and grocery delivery, which launched earlier this year in the US, is now expanding to Europe. Laundry pickup and delivery is available in select US cities through a partnership with Rinse, with Airbnb guests receiving free pickup, delivery, and next-day rush service. Starting in November, baby gear rentals, including cribs, strollers, high chairs, and toys, will be delivered and set up at listings in more than 60 US cities through a partnership with BabyQuip, with Airbnb guests receiving 10% off. Additional services through local partners include ski and snowboard gear rentals in the French Alps and boat rentals in South Florida. Later this fall, Airbnb plans to add AI-powered tools for hosts, which the company says will give hosts greater control, clearer insights, and more time to focus on hospitality. A multi-listing calendar will let hosts update pricing, availability, cancellation policies, or discounts across all of their listings at once, or just a few, while interactive 3D floor plans will give guests a view of a home’s layout before they book. A dynamic pricing feature will recommend a price range and, with one tap, adjust nightly prices automatically based on daily demand and supply. Hosts can change their range at any time and can view or adjust prices directly in the calendar. An AI earnings dashboard will display AI summaries of a host’s performance and the factors impacting it, alongside suggested actions the host can take without leaving the dashboard. coreStoryFacts.text: Airbnb is adding new social features to its platform that allow guests attending experiences to communicate and keep in touch.

Business chief Dave Stephenson said the updated tech builds on the company's "vision for where to take Airbnb next." Users need to opt in to social features for every experience and can unsubscribe at any time, Airbnb said.
At the time of the May app overhaul, Stephenson told CNBC that Airbnb felt it had a "strong foundation" to expand its offerings.
The new updates add a direct messaging feature for attendees to connect with other guests and a pre-event dashboard that shows profiles of other participants attending the experience.
Earlier this year, Airbnb said it would invest $200 million to $250 million in a new business opportunities.
Airbnb also updated its artificial intelligence chatbot it started rolling out this year to answer personalized customer support questions.
The tool can now cancel reservations or adjust dates when prompted and is available in English, Spanish and French to users in North America.
Now, users can switch on a toggle to search for properties via text or voice prompts.
Once you start the search, the interface will show you dynamic filters based on your preferences.
For instance, if you type “baby” in the AI search filter, Airbnb will automatically show you further filters like cribs, playgrounds, or children’s books and toys.
Earlier this year, he teased the new search feature for property discovery .
The company is also doubling down on social features that nudge people to take more trips and book additional experiences such as food tastings and craft workshops.
Airbnb is evolving in two directions: On the ground, it wants to compete with hotels by providing myriad services; online, it is using AI and people in its Airbnb network to aid travel discovery.
Airbnb is also building pages about neighborhoods based on guest reviews and other sources to help travelers discover places to eat and things to do.

extraction.body: Airbnb is evolving in two directions: On the ground, it wants to compete with hotels by providing myriad services; online, it is using AI and people in its Airbnb network to aid travel discovery. As part of its fall product update, the company is adding services to the app it had launched last year, such as meal delivery, laundry, baby-gear rental, ski and boat rental in limited locations, and expanded grocery delivery. The second big feature is AI search. The company has taken a cautious approach to rolling out AI features, with CEO Brian Chesky opting to stay away from a chatbot-like interface . Earlier this year, he teased the new search feature for property discovery . Now, users can switch on a toggle to search for properties via text or voice prompts. Once you start the search, the interface will show you dynamic filters based on your preferences. For instance, if you type “baby” in the AI search filter, Airbnb will automatically show you further filters like cribs, playgrounds, or children’s books and toys. The platform is also using AI to bring out relevant features of a property, and will let you compare properties in your wish list by way of AI-powered summaries and reviews. “We are finally making our first foray into AI search. And what you see is just the very beginning of something. And over the coming months, we’re going to really be iterating this very quickly. It’s not hard to create AI search; it’s hard to create AI search in e-commerce when you have $100 billion going through your platform,” Airbnb CEO Brian Chesky told TechCrunch. “Anyone can vibe-code a search function, but to do something that doesn’t kill conversion rate, that’s the hard part.” The company is also doubling down on social features that nudge people to take more trips and book additional experiences such as food tastings and craft workshops. Last year, the app started allowing users to connect with fellow travelers and friends on its platform. Now, travelers can look at a map based on their connections’ past or upcoming trips. When you tap on a trip, you can see where your connection stayed, and which experiences they sought out. For those conscious about their privacy, there’s an option to not share their trips with others as well. Airbnb is also building pages about neighborhoods based on guest reviews and other sources to help travelers discover places to eat and things to do. Search results now include AI-powered listing descriptions highlighting key features of a home, and an AI-powered comparison tool displays homes from a user’s wishlist side by side, with AI summaries of their key features.

In its Help Center documentation , Airbnb states that AI-powered search considers factors including quality, popularity, price, and location, and that AI also supports personalization, customer support, and guest-host communications such as suggested quick replies for hosts.

sources.title: Instagram is adding an AI ‘assistant’ to tell you how to post
passages: The company announced Wednesday that its standalone Edits app will now include an AI “creative assistant” that pulls in data from a user’s Instagram account and offers suggestions on what to change.
Instagram is the latest social media platform to add built-in AI-powered features that will give users feedback on their posts.

Using the new assistant, creators can ask open-ended questions about what’s trending on Instagram, why one video worked and another didn’t, or what piece of content resonated most with their audience.
Now, both YouTube and Instagram are effectively promising to give creators personalized advice on how to ride the algorithm.
Instagram says it can spot patterns over time and give a creator suggestions that metrics alone can’t provide.

extraction.body: Instagram is the latest social media platform to add built-in AI-powered features that will give users feedback on their posts. The company announced Wednesday that its standalone Edits app will now include an AI “creative assistant” that pulls in data from a user’s Instagram account and offers suggestions on what to change. Using the new assistant, creators can ask open-ended questions about what’s trending on Instagram, why one video worked and another didn’t, or what piece of content resonated most with their audience. Instagram says it can spot patterns over time and give a creator suggestions that metrics alone can’t provide. Creators can also ask for ideas for content, how to hook viewers, what captions to use, which audio tracks are trending, and how to script videos. --- Are you a creator using platforms’ AI tools? Contact me at mia@theverge.com or at miasato.11 on Signal. --- If that sounds familiar, it’s because YouTube also just announced updates to its sprawling AI-powered dashboard that tells creators how to maximize engagement. (YouTube’s version, which it initially announced in 2025, also has AI editing and A/B testing capabilities.) If you’ve been online for a while — and especially if you’ve ever had to pay attention to social media metrics — you’ll know that this is quite a shift. Historically, many platforms have limited or even hidden detailed metrics about how your own content is performing. The platforms certainly have not been open about why a video or post performed poorly. Tools like CrowdTangle, which researchers and journalists used to monitor the most popular content on Meta platforms, have been shut down or restricted. Now, both YouTube and Instagram are effectively promising to give creators personalized advice on how to ride the algorithm. It’s in both the platforms’ and creators’ best interest to shape content for maximum engagement. As I wrote earlier this month, though, what happens when everyone is perfectly optimizing their content? Will content become even more similar as creators adjust to one another? The shift also raises interesting new questions about the relationship between tech companies and the creators that fill the platforms with things to look at: How does this dynamic change when platforms are straightforwardly giving creators instructions on how to post? The new feature is free for creators to use, up to a point. Meta says “power users” will be able to buy a Meta One subscription for more usage. In the end, it may end up re-creating the same frustrations and opaqueness that have plagued content creators for years — but this time, behind a paywall.

extraction.body: Home / How to Post on Multiple Social Media Platforms At Once Cross-posting used to mean pasting the same caption onto every platform and hoping it worked everywhere. In 2026 it means taking one piece of content and shaping the file, the words, and the timing to fit each channel, all from one place. You can post to all your social media at once without the copy coming out wrong on half of them. Sometimes you do that in a dashboard, and sometimes you ask an AI assistant to handle it, but either way the days of five open tabs and manual re-uploads are behind you. The word covers three different things that used to get treated as one: Old-school cross-posting handled all three the same way: copy, paste, publish. The 2026 version treats them separately, and the tools have caught up to that. Manual, One Platform at a Time: You upload to each app by hand, one after another. Most people still do this for their personal accounts, and it falls apart once you’re running more than a couple. The same things go wrong every time: a post you forgot, a caption that didn’t match, something that went up at the wrong hour because you got the timezone wrong. It’s fine for one or two channels and miserable by the time you hit four. A Scheduler That Adjusts Each Post: Metricool’s Planner is what most social teams use. You write the post once, tweak it for each network in the same editor, preview how it’ll look on each one, and schedule it for each platform’s best time. It’s the dull, dependable option, which is what you want when you’re publishing on a schedule. AI Assistants With a Connected Account: This is the newer mode. Metricool’s MCP server connects to AI assistants and automation tools, including Claude, ChatGPT, Cursor, Make, Zapier, and n8n. You ask Claude, “draft an Instagram caption, a LinkedIn post, and a TikTok script from this blog, and schedule them at each platform’s best time tomorrow,” and it does. Nothing publishes without your approval, but the drafting, formatting, and scheduling happen in chat. This is the mode teams are still figuring out, and it’s where you get the most time back. You don’t have to pick one. Most teams use the scheduler and the AI assistant together, depending on the job. Say you’ve filmed a five-minute product tutorial. Over the next week or two, it turns into: Metricool’s composer holds all of that in one draft. You upload the video once, adjust the cut and the copy per network, and see side-by-side previews before anything goes live. That’s one video turned into seven posts, all inside a single calendar entry. Handling this in native apps means seven separate uploads and no single view of what’s going out when. A basic scheduler that posts the same thing everywhere is only a little better, since you lose the formats each platform is built around. The Metricool MCP changes what you spend your time on. A few things that stop being manual work: You still make the calls on all of it. The copy-pasting and the manual data entry go away, and neither ever needed a person in the first place. Setup happens once. In Claude, you add Metricool from the Connectors Directory, or through Settings > Connectors > Browse connectors. In ChatGPT, you add it from the Apps section in the sidebar. Either way, you log in, grant access, and it becomes a conversation from there. Say you’ve published a long-form how-to on YouTube, a full ten-minute walkthrough. You want the highlights running as an Instagram Reel, a YouTube Short, and a TikTok, plus a written thread on Bluesky, X, and Threads. Here’s how to cross-post it with Claude connected to Metricool, and where the line sits between what you do and what Claude handles. What You Handle First: The video editing. Claude works with words and scheduling, not video, so cutting the vertical clip out of your ten-minute recording is on you or your editor. Export one strong 30-to-60-second segment, vertical, and get it into Metricool as an attachment. Everything after that, Claude can pick up. 1. Give Claude the Source: Paste the video’s transcript or point it at the YouTube link, and say what you’re making. 2. Ask for the Short-Video Captions: The clip is the same across Reels, Shorts, and TikTok, but the words around it shouldn’t be. Ask for all three at once. “Write three captions for the same clip: an Instagram Reel caption with a hook in the first line and a few hashtags, a YouTube Shorts title and description, and a TikTok caption. Keep the hook tight on all three since the clip is short.” Claude writes each one in the shape its platform wants. 3. Ask for the Thread: The written platforms want the how-to spelled out, not a clip. One prompt covers all three. “Now turn the main steps from the tutorial into a thread. Give me a version for X, one for Threads, and one for Bluesky. The first post has to stand on its own.” 4. Turn It Into a Carousel Too: A how-to breaks down well into a carousel, one step per slide, and it’s a good use of Claude. It can write the slide-by-slide copy straight from your transcript, which leaves you with the design instead of the wording. You still build the slides, but the words are done. 5. Schedule It All: Claude schedules directly into Metricool through the MCP, at the times you name or at each platform’s best time. “Schedule the Reel, Short, and TikTok for tomorrow, and spread the threads across the next two days, all at each platform’s best time.” Claude stages everything and sends back a clickable link to each post. 6. Review Before Anything Publishes: Click any link to open the post in Metricool’s Planner. Check the clip’s crop, tweak a caption, fix the formatting. Nothing goes live until you approve it, and this is also where you’d handle any attachment or formatting detail Claude couldn’t set exactly. Once the clip is exported, the writing and scheduling take about ten minutes. The first run is slower while you work out how you like to ask, and after that it’s a routine you can run between meetings. Not everything wants to be duplicated. Some cases are worth publishing to one platform and stopping: A good cross-posting workflow makes it easy to opt out per channel. In the Planner, deselecting a network from a post takes one click. Through Claude, it’s a sentence: “skip LinkedIn on this one.” Most teams settle into a similar setup, and the cross-posting tools worth building it around share a few traits: Shape a post once and adapt it per network in the same editor, then schedule each one for its best time. Save time and take control of your social media strategy with Metricool. Schedule posts, track performance, and manage all your accounts effortlessly. Meta also isn't using private messages on its platforms to train the new model, Clegg told the outlet.

Meta has some measures to exclude private details from public datasets used by the AI, Clegg told Reuters.

extraction.body: Meta has been using public Facebook and Instagram posts to train its new artificial intelligence assistant, a spokesperson said. Posts that were fed to the new AI include both text and photos, Nick Clegg, Meta's president of global affairs, told Reuters in a Thursday interview. However, the AI hasn't touched private posts, like those shared only with friends and family, Clegg said, per Reuters. Meta has some measures to exclude private details from public datasets used by the AI, Clegg told Reuters. Meta also isn't using private messages on its platforms to train the new model, Clegg told the outlet. "We've tried to exclude datasets that have a heavy preponderance of personal information," Clegg said, per Reuters. He added that Meta hasn't used sites like LinkedIn to train its AI due to privacy concerns. Meta opened its virtual assistant, Meta AI, to the public on Wednesday in a Beta release. The new assistant is meant to help users create their own digital stickers based on text prompts, edit photos with text instructions, and chat with AI personalities like the rapper Snoop Dogg acting as a "Dungeons & Dragons" Dungeon Master. In this article, we'll explore some of Instagram’s newest features and what they mean to marketers. Instagram continues to be a powerhouse platform for marketers and Instagram creators, with recent statistics highlighting its importance: To maintain this relevancy, Instagram continues to evolve with new features designed to increase engagement, improve content creation, and facilitate easier communication between brands and their audiences. From enhanced Stories and Reel capabilities to new ways of interacting through Broadcast Channels and AI, these updates offer marketers new opportunities to connect with their audience and grow their presence on the platform. Let's explore five key areas where the Instagram app has introduced new features and how to use them to boost your marketing efforts. Instagram Stories continue to be a focus for the platform, with new features designed to boost engagement and interaction. Instagram's head, Adam Mosseri, noted that users spend more time sharing content privately, either in direct messages or stories. Instagram has introduced several updates to improve feed posts' functionality and engagement potential, making it easier for marketers to create compelling content directly within the app. You can now include up to 20 slides in carousel posts, up from the previous limit of 10. While this change has been in effect since 2024, the extended format is perfect for in-depth storytelling, comprehensive product showcases, or recapping events in detail. While this new feature is more basic than dedicated design tools like Canva, it's perfect for quick, on-the-go content creation. You can make text-based carousel posts or add captions to images without leaving the Instagram app. However, for more complex designs or brand-specific templates, you may still want to use external tools. This update also includes a scheduling feature, allowing users to plan their post schedule. While the current version is relatively basic, Instagram could add more templates and design options in the future, making it an increasingly powerful tool for content creators and marketers. These new interactive elements can be added to feed posts. They appear as small visual icons in white font at the bottom corner of the post, potentially showing how many people have participated. Want to encourage more followers to join your Broadcast Channel for exclusive content or updates? Feed posts can now include tags for broadcast channels, helping to drive more users into these community spaces. Instagram continues to invest heavily in Reels, introducing new features to enhance creation and editing capabilities. These updates make it easier for marketers to create high-quality, engaging, short-form video content directly within the app. The AI Business Society filters the noise for you, with expert-led training you can put to work the same day — plus a community of marketers sharing what's actually working. You can now add up to 20 different audio tracks to a single Reel, including music, sound effects, and voiceovers. Also, Instagram is testing a feature that allows subscribers to reply to specific messages within a Broadcast Channel, facilitating more focused discussions. If you can access this feature, use it to encourage more targeted conversations and gather feedback on specific topics or announcements. Instagram has integrated Meta AI , a conversational AI assistant, into the platform. This tool can help marketers with various tasks directly within the Instagram app. Users can access Meta AI through the Explore page to ask questions and get information. It appears as a search option with a purple and blue ring icon. You can use Meta AI to research hashtags quickly, get content ideas, or find information relevant to your marketing efforts without leaving the Instagram app. For example, you could ask for the top 10 hashtags in your industry or content ideas related to your niche. coreStoryFacts.text: The company announced Wednesday that its standalone Edits app will now include an AI “creative assistant” that pulls in data from a user’s Instagram account and offers suggestions on what to change.
Instagram is the latest social media platform to add built-in AI-powered features that will give users feedback on their posts.

Using the new assistant, creators can ask open-ended questions about what’s trending on Instagram, why one video worked and another didn’t, or what piece of content resonated most with their audience.
Now, both YouTube and Instagram are effectively promising to give creators personalized advice on how to ride the algorithm.
Instagram says it can spot patterns over time and give a creator suggestions that metrics alone can’t provide.
Cross-posting used to mean pasting the same caption onto every platform and hoping it worked everywhere.
You can post to all your social media at once without the copy coming out wrong on half of them.
A Scheduler That Adjusts Each Post: Metricool’s Planner is what most social teams use.
You write the post once, tweak it for each network in the same editor, preview how it’ll look on each one, and schedule it for each platform’s best time.
AI Assistants With a Connected Account: This is the newer mode.
Nothing publishes without your approval, but the drafting, formatting, and scheduling happen in chat.
Say you’ve published a long-form how-to on YouTube, a full ten-minute walkthrough.
You want the highlights running as an Instagram Reel, a YouTube Short, and a TikTok, plus a written thread on Bluesky, X, and Threads.
Here’s how to cross-post it with Claude connected to Metricool, and where the line sits between what you do and what Claude handles.
You upload the video once, adjust the cut and the copy per network, and see side-by-side previews before anything goes live.
That’s one video turned into seven posts, all inside a single calendar entry.
Check the clip’s crop, tweak a caption, fix the formatting.
Nothing goes live until you approve it, and this is also where you’d handle any attachment or formatting detail Claude couldn’t set exactly.
In Claude, you add Metricool from the Connectors Directory, or through Settings > Connectors > Browse connectors.
Either way, you log in, grant access, and it becomes a conversation from there.
Claude works with words and scheduling, not video, so cutting the vertical clip out of your ten-minute recording is on you or your editor.
Export one strong 30-to-60-second segment, vertical, and get it into Metricool as an attachment.

extraction.body: Instagram is the latest social media platform to add built-in AI-powered features that will give users feedback on their posts. The company announced Wednesday that its standalone Edits app will now include an AI “creative assistant” that pulls in data from a user’s Instagram account and offers suggestions on what to change. Using the new assistant, creators can ask open-ended questions about what’s trending on Instagram, why one video worked and another didn’t, or what piece of content resonated most with their audience. Instagram says it can spot patterns over time and give a creator suggestions that metrics alone can’t provide. Creators can also ask for ideas for content, how to hook viewers, what captions to use, which audio tracks are trending, and how to script videos. --- Are you a creator using platforms’ AI tools? Contact me at mia@theverge.com or at miasato.11 on Signal. --- If that sounds familiar, it’s because YouTube also just announced updates to its sprawling AI-powered dashboard that tells creators how to maximize engagement. (YouTube’s version, which it initially announced in 2025, also has AI editing and A/B testing capabilities.) If you’ve been online for a while — and especially if you’ve ever had to pay attention to social media metrics — you’ll know that this is quite a shift. Historically, many platforms have limited or even hidden detailed metrics about how your own content is performing. The platforms certainly have not been open about why a video or post performed poorly. Tools like CrowdTangle, which researchers and journalists used to monitor the most popular content on Meta platforms, have been shut down or restricted. Now, both YouTube and Instagram are effectively promising to give creators personalized advice on how to ride the algorithm. It’s in both the platforms’ and creators’ best interest to shape content for maximum engagement. As I wrote earlier this month, though, what happens when everyone is perfectly optimizing their content? Will content become even more similar as creators adjust to one another? The shift also raises interesting new questions about the relationship between tech companies and the creators that fill the platforms with things to look at: How does this dynamic change when platforms are straightforwardly giving creators instructions on how to post? The new feature is free for creators to use, up to a point. Meta says “power users” will be able to buy a Meta One subscription for more usage. In the end, it may end up re-creating the same frustrations and opaqueness that have plagued content creators for years — but this time, behind a paywall.
